title: Trinidad's 800 MW AI Data Centre Bet and Trump's Tax Threat | Across the Water, Ep. 22
lede: Trinidad and Tobago signed three memoranda of understanding with US firms on Jul 10, 2026, two of them for AI data centres: Ernst & Young's 300 MW project and Hummingbird AI's 150 MW facility, with a long-term option to 500 MW. Fully built, that is about 800 MW, roughly a third of the country's 2,366 MW of installed generation. On Nov 20, President Trump threatened a "tremendous tax" on US companies that build data centres abroad, with no rate, start date or legal basis announced. Jamaica's cabinet approved an exploratory MOU on Nov 15 with investors it has not named. This episode sets out the deals, the power and water arithmetic, and the political risk.
keyPoints: Trinidad and Tobago signed three MOUs with US firms on Jul 10, 2026, the first of their kind with a Caribbean country: EY intends to partner on a 300 MW data centre; Hummingbird AI proposed 150 MW with a long-term option to 500 MW and first operations targeted for Q1 2028; Pinnacle Steel would refurbish the Point Lisas steel plant (TTT; AP, Jul 2026).

Fully built, the two data centres would need about 800 MW, against national installed capacity of about 2,366 MW summed from the Ministry of Energy's plant list, or roughly a third of the system (Ministry of Energy; Prof Andy Knight via CNC3, Nov 21, 2026).

At a White House briefing on Nov 20, 2026, President Trump said companies would not be allowed to build data centres in other countries and that a "tremendous tax" would follow. He said he had not yet told his staff; no rate, start date or legal basis has been announced, and a federal tax would require Congress (AP, Nov 20, 2026; CNC3, Nov 21, 2026).

Jamaica is earlier still: the cabinet approved an exploratory MOU announced Nov 15 with an undisclosed group of investors. Information Minister Dana Morris Dixon said on Nov 18 there is "no investor coming" and no deal, and that the project cannot affect water systems or draw on the grid (Jamaica Observer; Jamaica Gleaner, Nov 2026).

The government's US$5 billion and 5,000-jobs figures cover all three projects and are conditional on due diligence; a petition for independent assessments drew over 13,000 signatures in 24 hours in July, and parts of the country are on weekly water schedules (TTT, Jul 11, 2026; CNC3, Nov 21, 2026; AP, Jul 12, 2026).
